title: How To Stop Students From Roughhousing
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens by acknowledging that roughhousing is a natural, even beneficial impulse in kids, citing research that it releases brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), improves cognition, and helps build friendships and resilience. Despite this, he argues it should still be banned at school specifically, because it can mask bullying, escalate into real fights, and cause injury through falls or collisions, distinctions that are hard to judge reliably from a distance. His solution is twofold: enforce a clear, consistently applied consequence the moment roughhousing starts, ideally backed by a school-wide recess behavior plan, and separately ensure students get ample structured exercise elsewhere in the day, since exercise is what actually delivers the BDNF benefit roughhousing would otherwise provide. He frames banning roughhousing without adding exercise as leaving a void that predictably fills with fights, bullying, and playground trouble.
points: Roughhousing is naturally beneficial for kids, releasing BDNF and improving cognition, mood, and friendship-building.
It should still be banned at school because it can mask bullying, escalate into real fights, or cause injury.
Enforcement should be immediate and consistent, backed by a school-wide recess behavior plan.
Banning roughhousing without replacing it leaves a void that fills with fights, bullying, and playground trouble.
Structured exercise (morning runs, movement breaks, sports leagues, after-school wrestling or jiu-jitsu) delivers the same BDNF benefit roughhousing would provide.
quotes: Kids are inclined to roughhouse. And they should be encouraged to do so.
Roughhousing releases brain-derived neuroptrophic factor (BDNF), which improves cognition and alleviates anxiety and depression.
What can look like innocent playfighting on the outside may actually be one student bullying another. In many cases, it can be difficult to determine the difference.
It’s not roughhousing necessarily that causes injury. It’s the accidental falls. Getting pushed off playground equipment. Tripping on cement.
The truth is, very few students get enough of it. It’s critical to their social, emotional, and academic development.

Because of safety and bullying concerns, you have no choice but to outlaw free-play roughhousing and playfighting from your school and classroom. But doing so also leaves a void that must be filled with exercise.
